title: The One Where Rachel Has A Baby

jokes.text: Ross: 'Yes. The hard part is truly over.' — said upon arriving at the hospital while Rachel is in labor
jokes.setup: Ross triumphantly declares they made it to the hospital in seven minutes as if the journey was the challenge
jokes.punchline: He calls this 'the hard part' when Rachel is about to endure hours of labor — massive irony delivered with complete obliviousness
jokes.explanation: Classic Ross obliviousness — the irony is sharp and perfectly in character. He's so proud of himself he genuinely thinks getting to the hospital fast was the challenge. The timing lands well as a cold-open punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can't believe we made it to the hospital in record time!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's great Ross. We've only been here for twenty minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We got here an hour ago.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I've been here since yesterday.

jokes.text: Monica and Chandler are already at the hospital when Ross and Rachel arrive, despite Ross's pride over making it in seven minutes
jokes.setup: Ross is boasting about his record-breaking seven-minute transit time
jokes.punchline: Monica and Chandler are already there having taken a simple cab, deflating Ross's entire pride
jokes.explanation: The reveal lands cleanly — Ross's obsessive test-runs made no difference. Monica's simple 'we took a cab' is the deflating punchline. Solid structural comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: How did they beat us to the hospital?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't know, maybe they walked.

jokes.text: 'How the hell did you beat us here?' / 'We took a cab. Did you walk?'
jokes.setup: Ross spent enormous effort doing test runs to optimize his route to the hospital
jokes.punchline: Everyone else simply took a cab and arrived at the same time, rendering his preparation absurd
jokes.explanation: The 'Did you walk?' is a sharp, economic retort. The joke works because it immediately deflates Ross's pride in his preparation. The pacing is tight and the comeback is punchy.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Okay, is there some kind of magic tunnel to this hospital?'
jokes.setup: Everyone seems to have arrived before Ross despite his careful preparation
jokes.punchline: Ross's exasperated, slightly unhinged 'magic tunnel' theory captures his wounded pride perfectly
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny escalation of his frustration. The 'magic tunnel' phrasing is a bit colorful but doesn't quite pop. Functional character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, that's what you get for doing 15 in a 25.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'Ross, you stay here and talk. I'm gonna go have a baby.'
jokes.setup: Ross is making small talk and socializing at the check-in desk while Rachel is in labor
jokes.punchline: Rachel's flat, matter-of-fact dismissal — 'I'm gonna go have a baby' — as if it's the most routine errand while Ross chats
jokes.explanation: Very economical line. The contrast between Ross's social chattering and Rachel's total pragmatism works well. Strong delivery implied by the writing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: They always save rooms for important people.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, you're in labor.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, what if the President was in labor?

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Man, if only you'd gotten here sooner.' — responding to the hospital having no private rooms
jokes.setup: Ross is frustrated they can't get a private room
jokes.punchline: Chandler's perfectly-timed dry dig at Ross's earlier obsessive seven-minute boast — recontextualizing it as meaningless
jokes.explanation: This is Chandler at his best — maximum economy, perfectly placed, and it's a callback that makes the earlier joke pay off. The irony lands hard because we've been set up for it. Short, devastating, well-earned.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What if I was the president?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, then the White House would probably be located somewhere in Florida.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'They're saving them for important people! What if I was the president?'
jokes.setup: The hospital says no private rooms are available
jokes.punchline: Rachel's entitled, increasingly unhinged logic — invoking the president as a comparator while in labor
jokes.explanation: Rachel's pregnancy-entitlement mode is in full swing. The joke is functional but leans on a familiar 'entitled person makes absurd comparison' structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: How much would it take to move us up the list?

dialogue.speaker: Nurse
dialogue.line: Sir, you're in a hospital waiting room. There are people ahead of you who are sicker than you.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, and do you have to be so nasty about it?

jokes.text: Ross: 'We'd be in a lot of trouble. You don't know where any countries are.'
jokes.setup: Rachel asks 'What if I was the president?'
jokes.punchline: Ross's immediate, deadpan response about her geographic ignorance — a sharp character-specific insult that's also self-aware
jokes.explanation: One of the cleaner jokes in the episode. It's very Ross — the academic snob can't resist correcting Rachel even mid-crisis. Fast, specific, character-integrated. The fact that it's also a credible put-down (Rachel IS notably not bookish) adds a layer.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm leaving! I'm not staying here anymore!

dialogue.speaker: Nurse
dialogue.line: Ma'am, you're in active labor—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't care, I'm going home!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I'm staying! Oh God, make it stop!

jokes.text: Rachel has a contraction mid-argument with the nurse, immediately reversing her position on the semi-private room
jokes.setup: Rachel has been loudly refusing the semi-private room and threatening to go elsewhere
jokes.punchline: A contraction hits and she immediately says 'like to see a semi-private room?' — total 180 in one second
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom reversal played well. The timing — mid-threat, contraction, instant capitulation — is structurally efficient. Visual performance implied makes it land bigger than the words alone.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm helping! I'm wearing the hospital gown!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, it goes in the BACK.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Yeah, it couldn't hurt to look.' — after the contraction forces their hand on the semi-private room
jokes.setup: Rachel has just caved due to pain and agreed to see the semi-private room
jokes.punchline: Ross's casually understated agreement — as if they still have leverage — while clearly they have none
jokes.explanation: A small beat that gets a mild chuckle. Ross's faux-nonchalance is very him but it's not especially memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Ross. I'm a paleontologist.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And I should probably mention upfront - I will somehow make this about me and create unnecessary drama.

jokes.text: Ross apparently tries on a hospital gown or does something silly — Rachel laughs and says 'Never done this before.' Ross replies 'Yeah, well, it looks great.'
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel are killing time in the labor room
jokes.punchline: Implied visual gag — Ross is wearing/doing something absurd in the hospital room (likely a gown) and playing it straight
jokes.explanation: Hard to fully evaluate without the visual. The transcript gives minimal context but the laugh from Rachel and Ross's deadpan 'it looks great' suggest a solid physical bit. Middle-of-the-road score given incomplete info.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Look, I don't want to intrude. You two probably want some privacy.

dialogue.speaker: Marc
dialogue.line: No, no, no! Come on, this is a group experience. We're all in this together.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Hi, I'm Ross. I'm here to ruin this magical day for you.' — introducing himself to their new roommates
jokes.setup: Ross walks into the shared room to meet their new roommates, expecting tension from sharing
jokes.punchline: Ross preemptively introduces himself as the person who will ruin things — meta-self-awareness about his own reputation as a buzzkill
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. Ross's self-deprecating intro is sharp and quotable. It works on multiple levels: he's aware he's being awkward, he's trying to defuse it humorously, and it's very true to character. 'Ruin this magical day' is a great phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Marc
dialogue.line: Come on, Rachel, let me take some photos of you in labor. It'll be beautiful!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No way. Absolutely not.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Actually, honey, it might be nice to have those memories.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, no!

dialogue.speaker: Marc
dialogue.line: Everyone's doing maternity labor shots now. It's very trendy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't care if it's trendy, I'm not—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: We could frame one for the nursery.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Fine! Fine! Just... make it quick.

jokes.text: Marc snaps a photo of Rachel in the middle of a contraction without warning
jokes.setup: Marc and Julie have been aggressively friendly and inserting themselves into Ross and Rachel's experience
jokes.punchline: Marc cheerfully photographs Rachel at her most uncomfortable moment — the ultimate intrusive overstep
jokes.explanation: Good cringe moment. The Disgustingtons (as Rachel later calls them) are a well-deployed device but this specific beat is more of a setup for the running gag than a standalone killer joke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh no, I'm having a contraction!

dialogue.speaker: Julie
dialogue.line: What? Oh my God, me too!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What do you mean you're having a contraction?

dialogue.speaker: Julie
dialogue.line: I don't know, you started it!

jokes.text: Julie claims to be having a sympathy contraction at the same time as Rachel
jokes.setup: Rachel is mid-contraction and in real pain
jokes.punchline: Julie loudly joins in claiming her own contraction — competing with the actual laboring woman
jokes.explanation: Funny escalation of the intrusive couple gag. Julie claiming to have a sympathy contraction is appropriately absurd and cringe-worthy. Works as an escalation beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Three hours? That's nothing. I once waited four hours for a table at Nobu. And let me tell you, a baby is way less attractive than the sea urchin.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: But seriously, they keep saying it's a miracle. A miracle? I've seen miracles. This is just a lot of screaming and fluids. Although, come to think of it, so was my last relationship.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Oh, wow. Three hours and still no baby. Ugh, the miracle of birth sure is a snooze-fest.'
jokes.setup: Three hours have passed and Rachel still hasn't had the baby
jokes.punchline: Joey's completely self-centered, impatient take — 'the miracle of birth is a snooze-fest' — total Joey worldview
jokes.explanation: Very Joey. His total lack of patience or reverence for the 'miracle of birth' framing is characteristically perfect. 'Snooze-fest' applied to childbirth is a great word choice. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We should have a baby.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What?!

jokes.text: Monica tells Chandler she wants to have a baby, framing it as wanting to 'freak him out' — but Chandler calmly agrees
jokes.setup: Monica announces she wants to try to have a baby, expecting Chandler to panic
jokes.punchline: Chandler's immediate calm agreement — 'Okay' — completely subverts Monica's expectation and her own joke
jokes.explanation: Smart double-reversal. Monica thinks she's pulling a prank on Chandler, but his genuine calm agreement means the joke is on her — and then plays further. Great use of character growth (Chandler-the-commitment-phobe has matured). The 'What's that now?' second beat is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm ready for a baby.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, well first we need to talk about your diet. You can't just eat pizza and coffee all day.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I eat other things.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Sandwiches.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's still not a balanced diet. And you need to start going to bed at a reasonable hour instead of staying up watching TV until 3 AM.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: But that's when the best infomercials are on.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Exactly my point.

jokes.text: Monica reveals she was 'screwing with' Chandler to hear his voice go 'high and weird'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just panicked about being ready for a baby after initially agreeing
jokes.punchline: Monica admits she engineered the whole thing just to get his voice to go high — the prank reveal
jokes.explanation: The prank reveal is well-constructed but the second reversal (Monica actually IS ready) is what makes the whole sequence work. This beat is the middle pivot — solid but sets up the real punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I was testing you! And look at me, my voice is all high because I'm excited!

jokes.text: Monica: 'Because I am ready to have a baby. I just want Joey to be the father.'
jokes.setup: Monica has reversed and admitted she actually IS ready for a baby, calling Chandler's bluff
jokes.punchline: She then drops 'I just want Joey to be the father' — a completely unhinged escalation designed purely to panic Chandler
jokes.explanation: The escalation triple-whammy lands perfectly. The sequence goes: Monica pranks Chandler → Chandler panics → Monica pranks again even harder. 'I just want Joey to be the father' is the kind of absurd escalation that gets the biggest laugh in the sequence. Monica's comedic ruthlessness is perfectly rendered.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I want to have a baby.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? Really?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I want Joey to be the father.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What?!

jokes.text: Chandler: 'What? Are you crazy?' followed by Monica: 'Right there! That's all I wanted!'
jokes.setup: Monica drops 'I want Joey to be the father'
jokes.punchline: Chandler's explosive reaction is exactly what Monica wanted — she celebrates the high-pitched panic
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the extended prank sequence. Monica's 'Right there! That's all I wanted!' is a great punchline — she achieved her mission. The callback is clean and the structure is tight.

jokes.text: Marc announces Julie's cervix is dilated 7 centimeters: 'That's about four fingers! Doctor let me feel it.'
jokes.setup: The obnoxiously oversharing couple returns post-exam
jokes.punchline: Marc gleefully announces intimate medical details including that the doctor let him physically feel the cervix
jokes.explanation: A strong cringe escalation. Marc's breezy announcement of medical TMI hits the right note of horrified discomfort. 'Doctor let me feel it' is the detail that makes the audience squirm.

dialogue.speaker: Marc
dialogue.line: Come on, feel my wife's cervix.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, that's okay.

dialogue.speaker: Marc
dialogue.line: Well, feel mine then, so you know the difference.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm good, thanks.

jokes.text: Marc suggests Ross feel Rachel's cervix 'and then feel mine to compare'
jokes.setup: Marc has just shared he felt Julie's cervix
jokes.punchline: Marc invites Ross to do a comparison feel — the ultimate escalation of the TMI couple gag
jokes.explanation: The escalation lands as one of the bigger laughs in the episode. The specificity ('feel mine to compare') is what elevates it past a generic cringe moment. Ross's immediate 'We won't be doing that' sells the reaction.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Am I interrupting?' — Nurse/Doctor enters. Rachel: 'Yes! Thank you!'
jokes.setup: Rachel is trapped with the horrifying roommates and Ross has just been asked to feel a cervix
jokes.punchline: Rachel desperately welcomes the interruption as a rescue — 'Yes! Thank you!' with relief
jokes.explanation: Solid reaction beat. Rachel's enthusiastic 'Yes! Thank you!' is a good audience surrogate moment — we're all as desperate for relief as she is. Standard sitcom fare but executed well.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Geller
dialogue.line: Ross, I want to give you something. It was my mother's, and her mother's before that.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Mom, this is beautiful, but I'm not getting married.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Geller
dialogue.line: I know, I just thought you might want to have it, in case you ever do.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait... are you proposing to me?

jokes.text: Rachel: 'Ross? Ross? My child has no father!'
jokes.setup: Ross escapes to follow the nurse/doctor, leaving Rachel with the awful roommates
jokes.punchline: Rachel's dramatic, panicked cry — framing her abandonment with the roommates as her child having 'no father' — an absurd overstatement of the situation
jokes.explanation: Good comic desperation. 'My child has no father!' is a great overreaction to being left alone for two minutes — typical Rachel drama deployed for laughs.

dialogue.speaker: Judy Geller
dialogue.line: You know, Ross, when your father and I were your age, we didn't just live together. We got married. And let me tell you, the sex was wonderful.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Mom, please...

jokes.text: Ross's mom shows him his grandmother's engagement ring, asks him to give it to Rachel. Ross: 'Ma, you're asking me to marry you?'
jokes.setup: Ross's mom pulls out something to give him — context suggests it's a ring
jokes.punchline: Ross deliberately misreads the situation and jokes that his mother is proposing to him
jokes.explanation: Classic deflection-via-misread. Ross's joke is a way of avoiding the emotional weight of the conversation. Mildly funny but predictable as a sitcom beat.

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: Ross, if you don't start thinking about marriage, I'm going to have to tell you more about my sexual relationship with your father.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Mom, no!

jokes.text: Ross's Mom: 'Honestly, this isn't just some girl you picked up in a bar and humped.'
jokes.setup: Ross's mom is making a serious argument for why he should marry Rachel
jokes.punchline: She uses the word 'humped' — a jarring, hilariously inappropriate word choice from a mother making a sincere point
jokes.explanation: The word 'humped' from a Jewish mother making a serious argument is a genuinely funny incongruity. It's specific, surprising, and characterful. The word is doing a lot of heavy lifting — elevated by the deadly sincere delivery context.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: With Rachel, right?

jokes.text: Ross's Mom: 'Think about it. If you don't, I'll talk more about humping.'
jokes.setup: Ross says he can't deal with this now
jokes.punchline: His mom threatens more 'humping' talk as leverage — using her own awkward word as a comedic weapon
jokes.explanation: This is the stronger of the two 'humping' jokes. Using the word as a threat — 'I'll talk more about humping' — is a perfect callback escalation. It's economical, unexpected, and the idea that this would motivate Ross is absurdly logical. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You look amazing! I'm so attracted to you right now.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey, I'm pregnant!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Ross's dad, after learning Ross isn't with Rachel: 'Right. And with who again?'
jokes.setup: Ross explains he's not going to get with Rachel just because they're having a baby
jokes.punchline: His dad's sarcastic 'with who again?' — implying he can't conceive of a better option
jokes.explanation: Very economical parental snark. 'With who again?' is a dry, well-timed dig. Not a classic but efficiently delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, I know. I do this thing where I say stuff that makes people really uncomfortable, and then I act like I don't know why everyone's looking at me like that. But I do know. I always know.

jokes.text: Joey: 'She's like the perfect woman. I know she turned me down, but if she wanted to be with me, I would take her in my arms and...' — trails off wistfully
jokes.setup: Joey is commiserating about Ross not wanting to be with Rachel
jokes.punchline: Joey's eulogy for his own romantic failure — wistfully trailing off mid-sentence about what he'd do if Rachel wanted him — the absurdity of his own missed shot
jokes.explanation: Joey's wistful trailing off is funny because it's both sincere and completely self-centered — he makes Rachel's birth story briefly about his own romantic regret. Character-specific and gently sad-funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So what happened with that couple?

jokes.text: Joey: 'I haven't bummed you guys out like this in a while.'
jokes.setup: Joey has just delivered an unexpectedly sincere and sad speech about wanting Rachel
jokes.punchline: Joey's self-aware acknowledgment that he's been a downer — delivered with casual acceptance
jokes.explanation: Joey's self-awareness here is surprisingly sharp and very funny. The meta-acknowledgment that he's been a bummer works because it's true, he knows it, and he's oddly comfortable with it. Good economy.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'What happened to the Disgustingtons?'
jokes.setup: Ross mentions new roommates have replaced Marc and Julie
jokes.punchline: Rachel has named the horrible couple 'The Disgustingtons' — a fake surname that perfectly encapsulates her feelings
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'The Disgustingtons' is an inspired naming gag — it sounds like a real surname, encapsulates the disgust perfectly, and is immediately quotable. The casualness with which Rachel deploys it is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So this new couple I met uses the cutest pet names for each other.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: He calls her 'Dummy' and she calls him 'Idiot.'

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I thought it was so sweet until I realized... those are actual insults.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Not before she gave me a nice, juicy shot of little Jamie, crowning away.'
jokes.setup: Ross is explaining what happened when Julie was wheeled out for delivery
jokes.punchline: Ross's traumatized description of witnessing a crowning — 'nice juicy shot' delivered in a tone of horror disguised as cheerfulness
jokes.explanation: Good dark-ish comedy. The phrase 'crowning away' with 'nice juicy shot' is appropriately horrifying. Ross's trauma about witnessing childbirth is a solid running theme.

dialogue.speaker: Angry Woman
dialogue.line: You were looking at Rachel! Don't deny it!

dialogue.speaker: Husband
dialogue.line: I wasn't looking at Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Angry Woman
dialogue.line: Yes you were! And you were enjoying it!

dialogue.speaker: Husband
dialogue.line: I was not enjoying anything!

dialogue.speaker: Angry Woman
dialogue.line: Then why are you getting aroused by watching her go into labor?!

jokes.text: Ross describes the new roommates as having 'unusual pet names for each other — including Evil Bitch and Sick Bastard'
jokes.setup: Ross says the new couple has 'unusual pet names for each other'
jokes.punchline: The pet names are 'Evil Bitch' and 'Sick Bastard' — a violent, absurd reveal
jokes.explanation: Classic setup/punchline with great execution. 'Unusual pet names' perfectly primes the audience. The reveal of 'Evil Bitch' and 'Sick Bastard' as terms of endearment is a great subversion — implies a genuinely unhinged relationship, sets up the scene to follow perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Angry Woman
dialogue.line: This is all your fault! If you hadn't gotten her pregnant, she wouldn't be in this pain right now!

jokes.text: New Woman: 'She's in labor. You like that, you sick son of a bitch?'
jokes.setup: The couple is fighting through the curtain about whether the man was looking at Rachel
jokes.punchline: The woman adds the detail that Rachel being in labor makes the alleged looking somehow MORE depraved — total paranoid logic
jokes.explanation: Good sustained cringe. The 'she's in labor, you like that?' logic is hilariously broken and paranoid. Part of the larger running gag of this nightmare couple.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well, I'm warning you—

dialogue.speaker: Angry Woman
dialogue.line: You listen here, you paleontology nerd! My husband may be a lot of things, but he's twice the man you'll ever be, you fossil-faced, lab-coat-wearing, dating-disaster of a human being!

jokes.text: Ross timidly peeks through the curtain to try to intervene, then retreats as the woman adds 'fat pervert'
jokes.setup: Ross tries to be a peacemaker with the insane couple
jokes.punchline: He's immediately incorporated into the accusations as a 'fat pervert' and retreats — his attempt at diplomacy backfires instantly
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy inferred — Ross peeking and retreating is a good bit. 'Fat pervert' applied to Ross is an escalation of the couple's paranoia.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? I can't take this anymore. You two need to just... I don't know, give the baby to someone else.

jokes.text: New Woman: 'He's looking at me.' Then after a beat: 'Wanna live to see your baby?'
jokes.setup: Ross quietly tells Rachel the man isn't looking at her
jokes.punchline: New Woman either psychically hears or assumes Ross is looking — threatens his life as a consequence
jokes.explanation: 'Wanna live to see your baby?' is a legitimately great threat line — dark, specific, and funny because it weaponizes the happy occasion. Good escalation of the nightmare couple.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Because we're ready! We have a great apartment, we have jobs, we have each other... I mean, what more do we need?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A baby?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Exactly!

jokes.text: Rachel: 'Oh, good God! If you want a baby so bad, just go steal it!'
jokes.setup: The nightmare couple is mid-fight in the labor room
jokes.punchline: Rachel, in labor and exhausted, snaps with 'just go steal it' — practical advice delivered in a moment of complete exasperation
jokes.explanation: 'Just go steal it' is a great dark-comedy line from Rachel. It's the kind of desperation-born pragmatism that works perfectly from a woman in labor surrounded by lunatics. Economical and sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Maybe they're ready.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ready? Ready?! We don't even have a crib! We don't have a stroller! We don't have a diaper bag! Oh my God, oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm just messing with you. We're totally ready.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'It's not right! We're not ready for a kid!' — pause — 'I'm kidding. This is gonna be fun.'
jokes.setup: Monica has just said she might be ready to try for a baby
jokes.punchline: Chandler panics convincingly then immediately reveals he was joking — a callback to Monica's earlier prank on him, now he pulls the same move
jokes.explanation: Smart callback — Chandler has learned Monica's move and deploys it on her. The panic-then-reveal is structurally satisfying as a callback. Good character growth joke: even his comedic timing has become Monica-like.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What if the baby can see us?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: The baby can't see us.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Are you sure? Because I'm pretty sure that would be weird for the baby.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'I'm not comfortable doing this in front of the babies.' — referring to kissing Monica in the maternity ward
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are in the maternity ward getting excited about trying for a baby
jokes.punchline: Chandler's mock-prudishness about being intimate 'in front of the babies' — the babies are newborns in the nursery
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever. The idea that Chandler is embarrassed to kiss in front of newborns — who are obviously oblivious — is absurdist logic delivered with perfect deadpan. Very quotable. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We could have sex in the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's so clean!

jokes.text: Monica suggests they find a room. Chandler: 'Right here?' Monica: 'No, not here.' Chandler: 'Maybe here.' — they're in a hospital looking for a place to conceive
jokes.setup: Monica suggests they start trying for a baby right now
jokes.punchline: They immediately scheme to find a hookup location in the hospital — 'We're in a building full of beds! And it's so clean!'
jokes.explanation: Monica's 'full of beds! And it's so clean!' is a funny Monica-specific justification. Her Type-A practicality applied to a romantic moment is on-brand. The sequence is playful but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Come on, come on, come on...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yes! Yes! It's coming down!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Joey, it's just a chip.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Just a chip? Phoebe, I have been trying to get this chip for twenty minutes!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: This is a victory. This is my victory.

jokes.text: 'We've got time to kill. We're in a building that's full of beds! And it's so clean!'
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler want to find a place to 'try' in the hospital
jokes.punchline: Chandler's enthusiastic pitch of the hospital as a romantic venue, with his genuine appreciation of the cleanliness as a selling point
jokes.explanation: The addition of 'And it's so clean!' as a romantic qualifier is perfect Chandler — his enthusiasm for cleanliness as a seduction point is both specific and absurd. The exclamation marks suggest delivery that would sell this in front of a studio audience.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Could you press the button for me?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, you're standing right next to it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know, but I'm feeling very demanding today about really small things.

jokes.text: Joey fails to get food from a vending machine — 'Come on, you stupid machine!'
jokes.setup: Joey is waiting in the hospital, bored
jokes.punchline: Joey's food obsession manifests even in the hospital — the vending machine becomes an adversary
jokes.explanation: One of the weaker jokes. Joey's food obsession is well-established but 'angry at vending machine' is a lazy deployment of that trait. Minimal craft.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I was reading this book, right? And it said to do this thing, but there was a typo. So I did it wrong and fell down the stairs.

jokes.text: Phoebe meets a man on the elevator with a broken leg; she says 'I hate to be a ball-buster, but can I just do it?' referring to pressing the elevator button
jokes.setup: Phoebe meets an attractive man in the elevator who has a broken leg
jokes.punchline: 'I hate to be a ball-buster' used innocently about pressing an elevator button — Phoebe doesn't clock the double meaning
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe — she deploys an inadvertently loaded phrase with complete innocence. The setup of the broken-leg man makes the double entendre work. Solid.

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: Did some idiot cause your accident?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah... me.

jokes.text: Phoebe explains her broken leg came from 'a typographical error with a sex manual'
jokes.setup: The man asks how Phoebe broke her leg (she's on crutches or similar)
jokes.punchline: 'Typographical error with a sex manual' — a completely absurd explanation that opens more questions than it answers, in the most Phoebe way possible
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. It's perfectly Phoebe — only she could break a leg via a sex manual typo, and only she would mention it this casually to a stranger. The specificity ('typographical error') makes it funnier than a vague 'sex stuff' answer would be. Highly quotable, perfectly economical, and completely original in its absurdist specificity. Strong 8+ justified.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh no, wait! I need help pressing the button!

dialogue.speaker: Guy
dialogue.line: What button?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Any button! I'm trapped in here with you and I don't know which floor I need!

jokes.text: 'It's a long, embarrassing story. Let's just say, there was a typographical error with a sex manual.'
jokes.setup: Cliff (the man in the elevator) asks how Phoebe broke her leg
jokes.punchline: She explains it involved a typo in a sex manual — a premise so specifically weird that it implies an entire story the audience doesn't get to hear
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The specific detail of a 'typographical error with a sex manual' is simultaneously too specific and completely unexplained — it implies a story so absurd that your imagination runs wild. It is completely, specifically, only Phoebe who would (a) have this story and (b) treat it as routine. Perfect character integration, excellent economy. Comparable to our 8.0 anchor in quality.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Is she pregnant yet?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ross! It's only been three weeks! Everyone's going to have a baby before me. Everyone!

jokes.text: Man reveals HE broke his leg because he was an idiot on a cell not paying attention — 'Yeah. Me.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe sympathetically says 'Idiot on a cell not paying attention?' as an assumed cause for his broken leg
jokes.punchline: He confirms — 'Yeah. Me.' — he was the idiot
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word punchline. 'Yeah. Me.' delivers the reversal with absolute economy. Phoebe's sympathetic framing ('idiot on a cell phone') being confirmed as self-description is a clean subversion. The pause implied between 'Yeah' and 'Me' is crucial.

dialogue.speaker: New Woman
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh! I think I'm having a contraction!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: New Woman
dialogue.line: Wait, no, I'm fine. I'm having another one! Oh! Oh!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: How far apart are they?

dialogue.speaker: New Woman
dialogue.line: I don't know, like... thirty seconds?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's not how this works.

jokes.text: Clifford asks Phoebe if she wants to 'visit someone else' — the elevator doors close before she can respond
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Clifford have had a great elevator moment and he invites her to visit him
jokes.punchline: The elevator doors close right as she's about to respond — cutting off the connection. Phoebe screams 'Elevator! No!'
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom contrivance — the closing elevator doors is a well-worn device. Phoebe's desperate 'Elevator! No!' is energetically funny but the gag itself is very familiar.

dialogue.speaker: Nurse
dialogue.line: Oh, you're here to see Frank Jr.! He's in room 412.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yes, thank you so much!

dialogue.speaker: Nurse
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I can't let you in. Hospital policy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What? Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Nurse
dialogue.line: You're his half-sister. We can't have family members visiting unless they're on the approved list.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'She doesn't need to be [pregnant]. She'll still have the baby before I do.'
jokes.setup: A new woman is being brought in to the labor room; Ross wonders if she's pregnant yet
jokes.punchline: Rachel's bitter, paranoid certainty that ANYONE brought in will deliver before her — capturing her labor-room desperation
jokes.explanation: Very sharp. 'She doesn't even need to be pregnant' as a punchline captures Rachel's completely unhinged jealousy perfectly. Good character specificity — only a woman who has been in labor too long would think this way.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I'm a doctor. *clears throat* I'm afraid I have some bad news. You have... three days to live.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Three days?!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yes, three days. Unless... we operate immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, you're not a doctor.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm doing a bit here!

jokes.text: Julie claims to have another contraction in sympathy with Rachel — delivers it with dramatic 'Mm, mm... Oh, that was a big one.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has another painful contraction
jokes.punchline: Julie mirrors it with an exaggerated sympathy contraction, clearly not in real pain — 'Oh, that was a big one' — competitive suffering
jokes.explanation: Running gag that lands less well the second time — diminishing returns on Julie's sympathy contractions. The first was funnier. This one is more just checking the box of the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Do we have a condom?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Why? Oh! Oh no. Oh no, no, no, no, no.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We don't need a condom to get pregnant.

jokes.text: Julie from the previous room (the 'Disgustingtons') appears to have a mild contraction and says 'Mm, mm.' / 'Oh, that was a big one.'
jokes.setup: Earlier Julie co-opted Rachel's contractions; now she appears again minimally affected
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, that was a big one' delivered with almost no apparent distress — continuing to trivialize labor while Rachel is suffering
jokes.explanation: Extension of the running gag about Julie's suspiciously easy labor compared to Rachel's. Works as a contrast beat but isn't adding new comedic ground.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You should go talk to that guy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! So he should come talk to me?

jokes.text: Joey (as Dr. Drake Ramoray) to the hospital nurse: 'Dr. Drake Ramoray. It's Portuguese.'
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to use his soap opera doctor persona to get information about the man Phoebe met
jokes.punchline: Joey confidently explains the clearly-not-Portuguese name 'Drake Ramoray' is Portuguese — zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey/Drake Ramoray meta-humor. The claim that 'Drake Ramoray' is Portuguese is perfect — it's such a patently absurd assertion delivered with complete confidence. Only Joey could think this would work. High character integration score justified — this joke cannot exist without Joey's specific backstory.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, 3 centimeters? That's huge!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, 3 centimeters is barely an inch.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, the metric system is very confusing, okay? It's not my fault!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Actually, it kind of is.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Damn it! We're losing precious time. You want this man's blood on your head--' Phoebe: 'Hands.' Joey: 'Hands.'
jokes.setup: Joey is in full 'Dr. Drake Ramoray' mode trying to intimidate the nurse
jokes.punchline: Joey says 'blood on your head' — Phoebe corrects to 'hands' — Joey immediately accepts the correction mid-intimidation, breaking his own dramatic momentum
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The structure is perfect: Joey goes full intense-doctor-drama, makes a small idiom error ('head' vs 'hands'), Phoebe corrects him, and he docilely accepts — 'Hands' — instantly deflating his own big dramatic moment. The juxtaposition of intense urgency and compliant correction is very funny. Economy is superb — the whole joke is in that single-word exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: Wait, you're not really a doctor, are you?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? No, I was testing you! To see if you were paying attention.

jokes.text: 'You want this man's blood on your head--' / 'Hands.' / 'Hands.'
jokes.setup: Joey is doing a dramatic soap opera speech to guilt the nurse
jokes.punchline: He says 'blood on your head' (wrong idiom); Phoebe corrects him with 'Hands'; he accepts the correction mid-speech without breaking character
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-character joke. Joey's idiom error is organic (he's not smart), Phoebe's correction is delivered flat, and Joey's mid-performance 'Hands' acceptance — without missing a beat — is the comedic gem. The character integration is exceptional: only these two characters could produce this exact exchange. Near our 8.0 anchor quality.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't do math. I'm an actor!

jokes.text: 'Okay, okay. Making me sterile, but okay.' — Chandler, as they apparently find a broom closet or utility room to use
jokes.setup: Monica has found a place in the hospital for them to 'try' — apparently an unglamorous spot with harsh lighting
jokes.punchline: Chandler accepts the conditions with 'making me sterile, but okay' — acknowledging that the environment is literally working against their goal
jokes.explanation: Chandler's aside about being made sterile by hospital equipment while trying to conceive is a sharp irony. The deadpan acceptance ('but okay') is very much his register and the irony of the sterility joke in context is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So, um, how often do you... you know... with your girlfriend?

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, what? That's not really relevant to my allergies.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Right, right, no, it's... it's medical. I'm a doctor. So come on, just... ballpark figure.

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: I don't think—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And is she... I mean, would you say she's more of a... how do I put this... a "morning person" or a "night person"? In that way?

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm leaving.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait! One more thing—is she seeing anyone else? Medically speaking, of course.

jokes.text: 'Three.' / 'Just 3? I'm dilated 3!'
jokes.setup: Rachel expected to be 8 or 9 centimeters dilated after 17 hours of labor
jokes.punchline: She's only at 3 — worse than she was (she was 2 when they arrived). Her devastated repetition 'I'm dilated 3!' lands as the punchline
jokes.explanation: The deflation gag lands well because of the buildup. Rachel's repetition of the number as though saying it again might change it is a good characterization beat. The callback to the opening '2 centimeters' gives sharp viewers an extra layer.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So what are you into?

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: Oh, you know, the usual stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The usual stuff? Come on, there's gotta be something weird!

jokes.text: Rachel: 'I'm not waiting. I'm gonna push this baby out. I'm doing it. Three centimeters. That's gotta be like this, right?' [demonstrating with fingers]
jokes.setup: Doctor says Rachel is only 3 centimeters dilated after hours of labor
jokes.punchline: Rachel demonstrates what she thinks 3 centimeters looks like with her fingers — implying it's enough to push through
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy bit — Rachel's visual demonstration of centimeter-estimation is a good desperate-laboring-woman joke. The doctor's correction ('actually it's more like this') lands as the actual punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Ladies and gentlemen, I present to you... the guy who stole Phoebe's stuff!

jokes.text: Doctor: 'Actually, it's more like this.' [finger demonstration]. Rachel: 'Oh. Stupid metric system.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has incorrectly estimated what 3 centimeters looks like
jokes.punchline: Rachel blames the metric system — a completely wrong scapegoat deployed as an excuse
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. 'Stupid metric system' is a perfect punchline — it's completely illogical (centimeters are metric but it's irrelevant to her error), it's very American Rachel, and it's the kind of absurd blame-shifting that gets a big laugh. Highly quotable. Character integration is excellent — only Rachel would go there.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm going to sue the doctor personally, not the institution.

jokes.text: 'Actually, it's more like this.' / 'Oh, stupid metric system.'
jokes.setup: Rachel learns that 3 centimeters is actually larger than she thought
jokes.punchline: She blames the metric system — which Americans use in medical contexts — as though it's the system's fault for her ignorance
jokes.explanation: Rachel's reflexive blame of the metric system is perfectly character-specific — it's her kind of deflection, it reveals her obliviousness, and 'Oh, stupid metric system' is a highly quotable, economical line. The irony that medical centimeters are the only metric measurement most Americans use makes it extra funny.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm going to sue you!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, I'm not a lawyer.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, you are now!

jokes.text: 'Dr. Wells is a woman.' Joey: 'That was a test. Good response.'
jokes.setup: Clifford corrects Joey's claim that 'Dr. Wells sent me' by noting Dr. Wells is a woman
jokes.punchline: Joey recovers by calling it 'a test' — improvised damage control that he delivers with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: Very sharp recovery joke. Joey saying 'that was a test, good response' when caught in an error is characteristically Joey — total confidence in the face of being exposed. The 'good response' commendation is a perfect extra beat. High character integration because only Joey could deliver this without self-consciousness.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Oh my God! I'm so excited! I have the same condition!

jokes.text: Joey (as doctor): 'Age?' Clifford: 'Can't you figure that out?' Joey: 'I'm a doctor, not a mathematician.'
jokes.setup: Joey is asking routine medical intake questions but can't do basic arithmetic from a birthdate
jokes.punchline: 'I'm a doctor, not a mathematician' — a riff on the Star Trek 'I'm a doctor not a...' line, but also genuinely revealing Joey can't subtract years
jokes.explanation: One of the cleaner Joey jokes in this sequence. 'I'm a doctor, not a mathematician' works because it's plausibly doctor-speak while simultaneously revealing Joey truly can't calculate the age. The pop-culture echo adds resonance. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, no, no! Not in front of the baby!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Cover his ears! COVER HIS EARS!

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Oh. My. God.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Anything but that laugh! He'll be scarred for life!

jokes.text: Joey (as doctor): 'So 33 and single? Would you say you have commitment issues?'
jokes.setup: Joey learns Clifford is 33 and single
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately pivots from medical questions to what are clearly Phoebe's screening questions — breaking character while maintaining the frame
jokes.explanation: Good joke — the transparent shift from medical to romantic screening is funny because Clifford can clearly see what's happening. Joey's obliviousness to how obvious it is adds another layer.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: This is my husband, Sid. I'm so grateful for his skin problems that led to our meeting.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Do you sleep with women and never call them again?' Clifford: 'No.' Joey: 'Excellent. Excellent.'
jokes.setup: Joey is screening Clifford for Phoebe with increasingly non-medical questions
jokes.punchline: Joey's leading question is delivered with clinical gravitas — 'Excellent. Excellent.' like a satisfied doctor
jokes.explanation: Joey's double 'Excellent' in response to romantic screening criteria is good character comedy. The clinical repetition is funny — it sounds exactly like how a TV doctor would respond to a good test result, but applied to 'do you ghost women.'

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: My husband has a condition where he can only speak in questions.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That sounds difficult.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: How does he manage at work?

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Well, he's a lawyer, so it actually works out perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I guess that makes sense.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, okay, that's fine.

jokes.text: Joey: 'And, uh, finally, are you into any weird stuff, you know, sexually?' Clifford: 'No!' Joey: 'Ooh. Wrong answer.'
jokes.setup: Joey screens Clifford with one final question
jokes.punchline: 'Wrong answer' — Phoebe, via Joey, apparently WANTS some sexual weirdness, which is a great Phoebe-specific reversal
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode, possibly the best. The structure is perfect: the question itself is already funny (Joey asking this as a 'doctor'), but 'Wrong answer' completely subverts the expected punchline. The implication that Phoebe specifically WANTS sexual weirdness is perfect character comedy for her. It's shocking, economical, and deeply funny. 'Ooh. Wrong answer.' is immensely quotable. Justified 8+ — comparable to the anchor examples in structure and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: We're not getting married?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, Janice, you're not.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: But... but... OHHHHH!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is there any way to make that sound stop?

jokes.text: Joey: 'Enter Pheebs.' — having reported back to Phoebe like a field agent
jokes.setup: Joey has completed his reconnaissance mission and delivers his full report
jokes.punchline: 'Enter Pheebs' — Joey's completely casual, action-movie-style instruction for Phoebe to go in
jokes.explanation: Two words, well-deployed. Joey's operational swagger — 'Enter Pheebs' — treats the whole thing like a heist. Very Joey. Economy is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God! *NASAL LAUGH* Ohhhh!

jokes.text: Rachel's speech threatening to sue the specific nurse/doctor personally: 'I'm gonna sue you. My husband is a lawyer.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has been waiting through four women having babies while she's still at 3 centimeters
jokes.punchline: 'My husband is a lawyer' — Rachel's escalating threat deploys Ross as a weapon, implying they're married when they're not
jokes.explanation: Good Rachel moment — the entitled threat, combined with Ross not even being her husband, is a small gem. The 'Get back on that case, honey!' follow-up is the funnier beat.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Uh, Rach?' [correcting her]. Rachel: 'You get back on that case, honey!'
jokes.setup: Rachel calls Ross her 'husband' and a lawyer to threaten the medical staff
jokes.punchline: Ross starts to correct her ('Uh, Rach?') but Rachel dismisses him with 'You get back on that case, honey!' — using him as a prop while silencing his objection
jokes.explanation: Very good joke. Rachel deploying Ross as a legal threat prop while simultaneously shutting down his attempt to correct her is perfect Rachel comedy. 'You get back on that case, honey!' is delivered with delicious imperious authority. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: The new patient brought in turns out to be someone Rachel and Ross know — shock and disbelief
jokes.setup: Rachel begrudgingly allows a new patient to be brought in
jokes.punchline: The new patient is someone they know — the reveal is played for maximum impact ('Oh, my God!')
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom reveal. The transcript doesn't name who it is, but the reaction suggests it's played for maximum comedic shock. The long pause before the reveal (20:01 to 20:25) is structural comedy — the disbelieving silence.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'I mean, this is so great. We're gonna be baby buddies!' — to the new patient, through gritted teeth presumably
jokes.setup: Someone Rachel clearly has complicated feelings about is now sharing her labor room
jokes.punchline: 'We're gonna be baby buddies!' — forced enthusiasm that barely conceals horror
jokes.explanation: 'Baby buddies' as a phrase is funny on its own. The forced cheerfulness in the face of obvious horror is a classic cringe-sitcom beat. Works well.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Squeeze your legs together, cover the baby's ears.'
jokes.setup: Ross has just seen the new patient and realizes something problematic
jokes.punchline: Ross's impossible instruction to both contain the birth and protect the unborn baby from hearing something — an absurd mix of panic and protectiveness
jokes.explanation: Very funny line. The instruction to 'cover the baby's ears' when the baby is unborn is perfectly absurd — and the context of 'squeeze your legs together' adds to the pure panic. Good economy and originality.

jokes.text: The new patient's husband is introduced: 'I nabbed him at the dermatologist's. Thank God for adult acne!'
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel meet the new patient's husband Sid
jokes.punchline: 'Thank God for adult acne!' — a hilariously unglamorous origin story for their marriage/relationship
jokes.explanation: Great line. 'Thank God for adult acne!' is genuinely funny — specific, unexpected, and anti-romantic in a charming way. The dermatologist meet-cute is a clever subversion of rom-com origin stories.

jokes.text: 'You have to speak loudly. He's almost completely deaf.' Ross: 'Of course he is.'
jokes.setup: Ross tries to congratulate Sid
jokes.punchline: Sid is almost completely deaf — one more absurdity added to this impossible day. Ross's 'Of course he is' is the perfect resigned response
jokes.explanation: Ross's 'Of course he is' is a great resigned-acceptance line. It captures perfectly the feeling of a universe conspiring against you. The escalating absurdity of the roommate situation finding one more wrinkle lands well.

jokes.text: 'Of course he is.' — Ross or Monica's flat reaction to Sid being deaf
jokes.setup: Janice has just revealed her husband is almost completely deaf
jokes.punchline: 'Of course he is.' — the response that perfectly captures what everyone is thinking
jokes.explanation: Three words that function as the button on the deaf husband joke. The economy is exceptional — 'Of course he is' is the audience's collective response articulated. It doesn't add information; it validates the feeling. Perfect comic punctuation.

jokes.text: New Patient: 'Oh. Well, then shut me up.' Ross/Rachel: 'Just tell me how.'
jokes.setup: New patient says something embarrassing about their unmarried status and says 'shut me up'
jokes.punchline: The implied 'just tell me how' — either Ross or Rachel genuinely wishes they could shut her up
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh at the end of an awkward exchange. The 'just tell me how' response is functional but not memorable.

tmdb_overview:
Ross and Rachel go to the hospital to have their baby, but it's a long labor. They get stuck in a semi-private room, and many other couples come and go before Rachel is ready to deliver - the last couple being Janice and her new husband. Meanwhile, Chandler and Monica decide to start trying to have a baby, but can't find an empty hospital room where they wouldn't be disturbed. Also, Phoebe meets a handsome stranger and "recruits" Dr. Drake Ramoray to gather some personal information about him.

After Rachel gives birth to her little baby girl, she must confront relationship issues around her. So does Ross, who gets an engagement ring from his mother, while she urges him to propose to Rachel. The things, however, take an interesting turn.
insight: Finale's emotional weight dampens laughs: 65.9 score marks season's lowest density at 3.28 JPM.
